igcse-0580-tv-translations.description: Move every vertex by the same column vector, then describe or reverse the movement.

sections.title: How do the two entries tell me where to go?
sections.label: Read the column

blocks.html: The top entry of a column vector is the horizontal movement. The lower entry is the vertical movement. Positive means right or up, and negative means left or down.

figure.alt: Coordinate grid. A at (1,-1). B at (3,-1). C at (2,2). A′ at (7,5). B′ at (9,5). C′ at (8,8).
figure.caption: The same move takes each original vertex to its corresponding image vertex.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Move one vertex at a time, then join corresponding image vertices in the same order. A translation preserves the shape, size and orientation.

blocks.title: Translate a triangle
blocks.prompt: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(2,0),\quad B(5,0),\quad C(3,4)\). Translate it by \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-7\end{pmatrix}\). Give all three image vertices.
blocks.hint: Read the top component as the horizontal move and the bottom as the vertical one.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal move is \(2\) and the vertical move is \(-7\).

Make this same move from each vertex, then join the corresponding vertices in the original order.

The coordinates are \((4,-7),\;(7,-7),\;(5,-3)\).

retry.feedback: This is one translated vertex. Apply the same move to the other two vertices.

blocks.html: Read across first, then up or down. Swapping the two entries gives a different move.

blocks.title: Read the translation from corresponding points
blocks.prompt: A translation takes \(P(-1,1)\) to \(P'(-3,6)\). Find its column vector. Enter the components as an ordered pair.
blocks.hint: Measure the directed move from the original point to its image.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the original coordinates from the image coordinates. Use x first and y second.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: That moves backwards from the image to the original. Reverse the direction.

sections.title: How do I find the vector from two corresponding points?
sections.label: Describe the move

blocks.html: Choose matched points and compare their x-coordinates and y-coordinates from object to image.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Subtract the old coordinate from the new coordinate in each direction. Check a second corresponding pair if both shapes are shown.

blocks.title: Give a complete translation description
blocks.prompt: A single transformation takes triangle \(A(-1,0),\quad B(1,0),\quad C(0,3)\) to \(A′(4,-9),\quad B′(6,-9),\quad C′(5,-6)\). Which description is correct?
blocks.hint: Compare all corresponding pairs to check that their directed movements match.
blocks.solution:
The same directed move takes each original vertex to its image. That identifies a translation.

Each horizontal change is \(5\) and each vertical change is \(-9\).

retry.feedback: This takes the image back to the object. Compare object to image.
Keep horizontal movement on top and vertical movement below it.
A reflection in the x-axis does not change horizontal positions. Check how all the vertices move here.

blocks.html: Give the name of the transformation as well as the vector when asked to describe a translation fully.

blocks.title: Read the translation from corresponding points
blocks.prompt: A translation takes \(P(-7,-1)\) to \(P'(-13,5)\). Find its column vector. Enter the components as an ordered pair.
blocks.hint: Measure the directed move from the original point to its image.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the original coordinates from the image coordinates. Use x first and y second.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-6\\6\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: That moves backwards from the image to the original. Reverse the direction.

sections.title: How can I undo a translation?
sections.label: Reverse the move

blocks.html: To return to the original point, reverse the horizontal and the vertical movements.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Subtract the original translation vector from the image coordinates. You can also translate by the vector with both signs changed.

blocks.title: Find the point before a translation
blocks.prompt: A translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-8\end{pmatrix}\) takes a point to \((-1,-6)\). Find the original point.
blocks.hint: Undo the movement by changing both signs.
blocks.solution:
Reverse both components of the movement. The reverse vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-3\\8\end{pmatrix}\).

Apply that reverse movement to the image.

The coordinates are \((-4,2)\).

retry.feedback: You moved forward from the image. Use the reverse vector.

blocks.html: Subtract a negative component carefully. It moves the point in the opposite direction.

retry.feedback: That moves backwards from the image to the original. Reverse the direction.

How do the two entries tell me where to go?

The top entry of a column vector is the horizontal movement. The lower entry is the vertical movement. Positive means right or up, and negative means left or down.

Move one vertex at a time, then join corresponding image vertices in the same order. A translation preserves the shape, size and orientation.

Choose matched points and compare their x-coordinates and y-coordinates from object to image.

Subtract the old coordinate from the new coordinate in each direction. Check a second corresponding pair if both shapes are shown.

How can I undo a translation?

To return to the original point, reverse the horizontal and the vertical movements.

Subtract the original translation vector from the image coordinates. You can also translate by the vector with both signs changed.

Quick worked example

Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(1,-1),\quad B(3,-1),\quad C(2,2)\). Translate it by \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\6\end{pmatrix}\). Give all three image vertices.

The horizontal move is \(6\) and the vertical move is \(6\).

Make this same move from each vertex, then join the corresponding vertices in the original order.

The coordinates are \((7,5),\;(9,5),\;(8,8)\).

igcse-0580-tv-reflections.description: Reflect points and shapes in axis-parallel mirrors and give the equation of the mirror line.

sections.title: How do I use a mirror line on the grid?
sections.label: Perpendicular distance

blocks.html: The mirror line lies halfway along the perpendicular segment from a point to its reflection.

figure.alt: Coordinate grid. A at (3,3). B at (6,3). C at (4,7). A′ at (3,-1). B′ at (6,-1). C′ at (4,-5). Dashed lines show the guide construction.
figure.caption: Each pair of corresponding vertices is the same perpendicular distance from the mirror.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: For a vertical line, count horizontally to the mirror and continue the same number of units on the other side. For a horizontal line, count vertically.

blocks.title: Reflect a triangle in an axis-parallel line
blocks.prompt: Reflect triangle ABC with vertices \(A(4,-3),\quad B(6,-3),\quad C(5,-1)\) in the line \(x=2\). Enter the three image vertices.
blocks.hint: The mirror line is halfway between each vertex and its image.
blocks.solution:
Measure the distance to the mirror line \(x=2\) along the perpendicular grid direction.

Place each corresponding image point the same distance from the line on the opposite side.

The coordinates are \((0,-3),\;(-2,-3),\;(-1,-1)\).

retry.feedback: That is one reflected vertex. Give the full set of image points.

blocks.html: Do not count along the mirror itself. Move at right angles to it.

blocks.title: Recognise a point that stays fixed
blocks.prompt: What is the image of \((2,11)\) under reflection in \(x=2\)?
blocks.hint: Check whether the point lies on the given mirror line.
blocks.solution:
The point lies on the mirror line, so its perpendicular distance from the line is zero. It stays fixed.

The coordinates are \((2,11)\).

sections.title: How can I find the mirror line from an object and image?
sections.label: Recognise the mirror

blocks.html: Join a point to its image. The mirror passes through the midpoint of this segment and is perpendicular to it.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: When only x changes, the mirror is vertical and its equation starts with x. When only y changes, it is horizontal and its equation starts with y.

blocks.title: Find the position of the mirror line
blocks.prompt: A reflection in a horizontal line maps \((5,11)\) to \((5,1)\). Give the full description.
blocks.hint: The fixed coordinate tells you whether the movement was horizontal or vertical.
blocks.solution:
Only the y-coordinate changes. The mirror is perpendicular to the segment joining the points.

The changing coordinate is halfway between its original and image values, giving \(y=6\).

retry.feedback: Check which coordinate changes under this reflection.
The line must be halfway between the two points.
Use the midpoint of the changing coordinates.

blocks.html: Write a line such as x = 3 as an equation, using the coordinate that is fixed along the entire line.

blocks.title: Reflect a triangle in an axis-parallel line
blocks.prompt: Reflect triangle ABC with vertices \(A(3,-1),\quad B(6,-1),\quad C(4,2)\) in the line \(y=-3\). Enter the three image vertices.
blocks.hint: The mirror line is halfway between each vertex and its image.
blocks.solution:
Measure the distance to the mirror line \(y=-3\) along the perpendicular grid direction.

Place each corresponding image point the same distance from the line on the opposite side.

The coordinates are \((3,-5),\;(6,-5),\;(4,-8)\).

retry.feedback: That is one reflected vertex. Give the full set of image points.

sections.title: What if the vertex already lies on the mirror?
sections.label: Test a fixed point

blocks.html: A point on the mirror has zero perpendicular distance from it. The point remains in exactly the same place after reflection.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: After reflecting each vertex, check lengths and orientation. The reflected image is the same size with its orientation reversed.

igcse-0580-tv-rotations.description: Use quarter-turns and half-turns about Core centres and fully describe a rotation.

sections.title: How do I make a quarter-turn on a grid?
sections.label: Quarter turn

blocks.html: Find the centre and imagine an arm from it to a vertex. The arm changes direction by a quarter-turn and keeps the same length.

figure.caption: The centre stays fixed, and every vertex keeps its distance from it.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use tracing paper or count the relative steps from the centre. For an anticlockwise quarter-turn, an arm pointing right turns up. Check the sense before marking the image.

blocks.title: Rotate a shape about a stated centre
blocks.prompt: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(-1,-3),\quad B(2,-3),\quad C(0,0)\). Rotate it through \(90^\circ\) clockwise about vertex A \((-1,-3)\). Give the three image vertices.
blocks.hint: Measure relative to the given centre before turning. The distance from the centre stays the same.
blocks.solution:
For each vertex, count its horizontal and vertical steps from the centre of rotation.

Turn that relative movement through \(90^\circ\) clockwise and add the centre back. Join the rotated vertices.

The coordinates are \((-1,-3),\;(-1,-6),\;(2,-4)\).

retry.feedback: This is one rotated vertex. Give all three image points.

blocks.html: Read the centre from the question. Turning round the origin gives a different image when the centre is elsewhere.

blocks.title: Describe the centre, angle and direction
blocks.prompt: Triangle \(A(1,-1),\quad B(4,-1),\quad C(2,1)\) maps to \(A′(1,-1),\quad B′(1,2),\quad C′(-1,0)\) by a rotation. Which description is complete and correct?
blocks.hint: Compare two rays from the fixed vertex.
blocks.solution:
A and A′ are at the same point \((1,-1)\). This point stays fixed.

The line from A to B turns through \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise to reach the line from A′ to B′.

retry.feedback: The centre is correct. Check the angle and sense of the turn.
Vertex A is fixed and the shape turns around it.
The fixed vertex A identifies the centre in this case.

sections.title: How do I rotate about a vertex or midpoint?
sections.label: Hold the centre

blocks.html: Locate the centre first. If it is a midpoint, mark it halfway between the two given vertices. Leave the centre in place.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Rotate each relative movement from this centre. For a half-turn, the image lies the same distance on the opposite side of the centre.

blocks.title: Rotate a shape about a stated centre
blocks.prompt: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(3,-3),\quad B(5,-3),\quad C(4,-1)\). Rotate it through \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise about the origin \((0,0)\). Give the three image vertices.
blocks.hint: Measure relative to the given centre before turning. The distance from the centre stays the same.
blocks.solution:
For each vertex, count its horizontal and vertical steps from the centre of rotation.

Turn that relative movement through \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise and add the centre back. Join the rotated vertices.

The coordinates are \((3,3),\;(3,5),\;(1,4)\).

retry.feedback: This is one rotated vertex. Give all three image points.

blocks.html: A centre can lie on an edge. It only stays in the same place itself, not the entire edge.

blocks.title: Describe the centre, angle and direction
blocks.prompt: Triangle \(A(-2,-1),\quad B(0,-1),\quad C(-1,3)\) maps to \(A′(-2,-1),\quad B′(-2,-3),\quad C′(2,-2)\) by a rotation. Which description is complete and correct?
blocks.hint: Compare two rays from the fixed vertex.
blocks.solution:
A and A′ are at the same point \((-2,-1)\). This point stays fixed.

The line from A to B turns through \(90^\circ\) clockwise to reach the line from A′ to B′.

retry.feedback: The centre is correct. Check the angle and sense of the turn.
Vertex A is fixed and the shape turns around it.
The fixed vertex A identifies the centre in this case.

sections.title: What do I include in a full description?
sections.label: Describe the turn

blocks.html: A full description uses the name rotation, the centre, the angle and the direction when the directions differ.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use a corresponding ray from the centre to compare its before and after directions. A \(180^\circ\) turn has the same result in either sense.

blocks.title: Describe the centre, angle and direction
blocks.prompt: Triangle \(A(0,-3),\quad B(3,-3),\quad C(1,1)\) maps to \(A′(0,-3),\quad B′(0,-6),\quad C′(4,-4)\) by a rotation. Which description is complete and correct?
blocks.hint: Compare two rays from the fixed vertex.
blocks.solution:

revision.body:
How do I make a quarter-turn on a grid?

Find the centre and imagine an arm from it to a vertex. The arm changes direction by a quarter-turn and keeps the same length.

Use tracing paper or count the relative steps from the centre. For an anticlockwise quarter-turn, an arm pointing right turns up. Check the sense before marking the image.

How do I rotate about a vertex or midpoint?

Locate the centre first. If it is a midpoint, mark it halfway between the two given vertices. Leave the centre in place.

Rotate each relative movement from this centre. For a half-turn, the image lies the same distance on the opposite side of the centre.

What do I include in a full description?

A full description uses the name rotation, the centre, the angle and the direction when the directions differ.

Use a corresponding ray from the centre to compare its before and after directions. A \(180^\circ\) turn has the same result in either sense.

Quick worked example

Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(-2,-4),\quad B(0,-4),\quad C(-1,-2)\). Rotate it through \(90^\circ\) clockwise about the origin \((0,0)\). Give the three image vertices.

For each vertex, count its horizontal and vertical steps from the centre of rotation.

Turn that relative movement through \(90^\circ\) clockwise and add the centre back. Join the rotated vertices.

The coordinates are \((-4,2),\;(-4,0),\;(-2,1)\).

  • Give all details required in your description.

sections.title: How do I reflect across a diagonal or oblique line?
sections.label: Reflect across a diagonal

blocks.html: Use the perpendicular to the mirror through the vertex. Find the perpendicular foot, then continue the same distance beyond it.

figure.alt: Coordinate grid. A at (2,4). B at (4,4). C at (3,8). A′ at (-1,1). B′ at (-1,-1). C′ at (-5,0). Dashed lines show the guide construction.
figure.caption: The joins from the original points to their images meet the diagonal mirror at right angles.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: For a diagonal on a square grid, the perpendicular is the other diagonal direction. For a general straight line, use a constructed right angle or a known perpendicular foot.

blocks.title: Reflect in a diagonal mirror
blocks.prompt: Reflect triangle ABC with vertices \(A(3,5),\quad B(6,5),\quad C(4,7)\) in \(y=x+4\). Give its image vertices.
blocks.hint: Count along diagonals perpendicular to the mirror, not along horizontal rows.
blocks.solution:
For each vertex, follow a perpendicular to \(y=x+4\). For this diagonal, the perpendicular uses a slope of \(-1\).

Carry that same perpendicular distance beyond the mirror to mark the new point. Repeat for all three vertices.

The coordinates are \((1,7),\;(1,10),\;(3,8)\).

retry.feedback: Give all three reflected image points.

blocks.html: The horizontal distance is not the perpendicular distance for an oblique mirror.

blocks.hint: The foot M is halfway along the segment from P to its reflection.
blocks.solution:
The mirror passes through the midpoint of the segment joining P to its image.

Repeat the directed movement from P to M once from M. This puts the image the same distance beyond \(M\) along the perpendicular.

The coordinates are \((-4,-7)\).

retry.feedback: The foot is only halfway to the image. Continue the same distance beyond it.

How do I reflect across a diagonal or oblique line?

Use the perpendicular to the mirror through the vertex. Find the perpendicular foot, then continue the same distance beyond it.

For a diagonal on a square grid, the perpendicular is the other diagonal direction. For a general straight line, use a constructed right angle or a known perpendicular foot.

revision.body:
What changes if I reverse the arrow?

The first letter of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is the start and the second is the end. Its components are obtained from end minus start.

Reversing the arrow changes the signs of both components and keeps the length.

How do I add or subtract two vectors?

To add, put the tail of the next arrow at the head of the first. The resultant goes directly from the original start to the final end.

Add matching components. To subtract a vector, reverse both of its signs and add the reversed vector.

What does a scalar do to a vector?

A scalar multiplies both components. A positive scalar keeps the direction. A negative scalar points in the opposite direction.

Apply any scalars first, then add or subtract the resulting components. State the complete column vector.

Start at A and travel to B. Subtract the coordinates of A from those of B.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\7\end{pmatrix}\).

sections.title: Which arrows start at the origin?
sections.label: Separate starts and ends

blocks.html: A position vector always starts at the origin. A displacement between two points starts at the named first point and may not touch the origin.

figure.alt: Coordinate grid. O at (0,0). S at (-3,1). T at (-5,6). U at (0,13). Arrowheads mark the directed movements.
figure.caption: Position vectors start at O. The directed displacement from S to U starts at S.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use end position minus start position. This combines the backwards journey to the origin with the forward journey to the end point.

blocks.title: Distinguish a position from a displacement
blocks.prompt: Points S, T and U have position vectors \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\7\end{pmatrix}\), \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\8\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\) respectively. Find the directed displacement \(\overrightarrow{SU}\).
blocks.hint: Join S to O and O to U mentally, then add the resulting movements.
blocks.solution:
A position vector starts at the origin. The displacement starts at S, so subtract the position of S from the position of U.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: That is the displacement from U to S.
This position starts at the origin rather than S.

blocks.html: The named endpoint and the displacement can have different components even though they finish at the same point.

blocks.title: Use a route through the origin
blocks.prompt: In triangle OAB, \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\). Start at A, go to O, then to B. Express \(6\overrightarrow{AB}\) in terms of \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\).
blocks.hint: Travel backwards from the starting point to O before moving out to the finishing point.
blocks.solution:
The journey to O is the reverse of the position vector of A.

Add the position vector of B and scale the whole displacement by 6.

The vector is \(-6\mathbf{a}+6\mathbf{b}\).

retry.feedback: You reversed the route. Read its first letter as the starting point.
The first leg goes towards O. Its arrow reverses the starting position vector.

sections.title: How do I write a route using two directions?
sections.label: Follow a route

blocks.html: Follow a known route and add its movements. Reverse the sign of any vector used in the opposite direction.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: If \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\), then \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a\).

blocks.title: Use a route through the origin
blocks.prompt: In triangle OAB, \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\). Start at B, go to O, then to A. Express \(2\overrightarrow{BA}\) in terms of \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\).
blocks.hint: Travel backwards from the starting point to O before moving out to the finishing point.
blocks.solution:
The journey to O is the reverse of the position vector of B.

Add the position vector of A and scale the whole displacement by 2.

The vector is \(2\mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b}\).

retry.feedback: You reversed the route. Read its first letter as the starting point.
The first leg goes towards O. Its arrow reverses the starting position vector.

blocks.html: Changing the order of the letters changes the sign of the displacement.

blocks.title: Find a midpoint position vector
blocks.prompt: M is the midpoint of \(AB\), where \(A(-4,1)\) and \(B(0,6)\). Find its position vector.
blocks.hint: The midpoint is halfway from A to B. Its vector starts at the origin.
blocks.solution:
Find the average of the two horizontal positions and the average of the two vertical positions.

The position vector of M starts at the origin and ends at this midpoint.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\\frac{7}{2}\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: That is the movement from A to M. Add A's position to reach M from the origin.

sections.title: What part of the full segment do I travel?
sections.label: Divide a segment

blocks.html: An internal ratio counts parts on both sides of the point. Add the two numbers to find the total parts.

figure.alt: Coordinate grid. O at (0,0). A at (8,2). B at (3,8). M at (11/2,5). Arrowheads mark the directed movements.
figure.caption: Travel from O to A, then the stated fraction of the way from A to M.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: To get a position vector, reach the first endpoint from the origin and then travel the required fraction of the full segment.

blocks.title: Write the position vector of an internal point
blocks.prompt: In triangle OAB, \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\). M divides AB internally with \(AM:MB=4:3\). Find \(\overrightarrow{OM}\) in terms of \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\).
blocks.hint: The denominator is the total number of parts in the whole segment.
blocks.solution:
The full segment has 7 equal ratio parts. So \(\overrightarrow{AM}=\frac{4}{7}\overrightarrow{AB}\).

Start at O, travel to A, then add \(\frac{4}{7}\) of \(\mathbf b-\mathbf a\). Collect the coefficients.

The vector is \(\frac{3}{7}\mathbf{a}+\frac{4}{7}\mathbf{b}\).

retry.feedback: That is the displacement from A to M. Include the initial leg from O to A.
The part measured from A controls the coefficient of b.

blocks.html: A ratio such as 2 : 3 gives two fifths from the first end. It does not give two thirds of the full segment.

The position vector of M starts at the origin and ends at this midpoint.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{5}{2}\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

retry.feedback: That is the movement from A to M. Add A's position to reach M from the origin.

revision.body:
Which arrows start at the origin?

A position vector always starts at the origin. A displacement between two points starts at the named first point and may not touch the origin.

Use end position minus start position. This combines the backwards journey to the origin with the forward journey to the end point.

How do I write a route using two directions?

Follow a known route and add its movements. Reverse the sign of any vector used in the opposite direction.

If \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\), then \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a\).

What part of the full segment do I travel?

An internal ratio counts parts on both sides of the point. Add the two numbers to find the total parts.

To get a position vector, reach the first endpoint from the origin and then travel the required fraction of the full segment.
